strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored problem: in-generation watermarking for discrete-token autoregressive image generators. Adapting red-green watermarking to AR image tokens and identifying token reconstruction fragility as the key robustness bottleneck is a useful contribution.

The proposed cluster-level watermark is simple, technically plausible, and well motivated: grouping nearby codebook embeddings makes verification less sensitive to perturbations that move an encoded image to a neighboring token.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this niche: three AR model settings, post-hoc watermark baselines, a concurrent AR watermark baseline where available, multiple perturbations, regeneration attacks, ablations over cluster count, watermark strength, green-token fraction, and hash prefixes.

Results support the main claim that clustering substantially improves robustness over token-level red-green watermarking, and that the cluster classifier further improves detection under strong perturbations while preserving reasonable FID at k=64.
Runtime analysis is useful and shows an important practical advantage: verification is much cheaper than inversion-based diffusion watermark verification.
weaknesses: The best-performing method relies on several choices that are tuned empirically, especially hash-prefix selection over the tested perturbations. This weakens the statistical interpretation of the red-green detector and may overstate deployment performance if the attack distribution differs from the tuning set.

The null-model discussion is incomplete for clustered image tokens. The paper itself observes that unwatermarked green-token ratios can deviate substantially from the assumed binomial distribution for some prefixes and low cluster counts, but the implications for calibrated p-values, false-positive guarantees, and deployment thresholds are not fully resolved.

The strongest robustness results use a perturbation-trained cluster classifier trained on 100k generated images and a predefined augmentation set. This is reasonable, but the paper sometimes frames the approach around training-free simplicity while the most competitive variant depends on attack-specific supervised training and may overfit to the evaluated perturbation family.

The evaluation is limited to class-conditional, left-to-right, discrete-token AR image models. It does not establish behavior for text-to-image AR systems, masked/parallel AR decoding, continuous-token AR models, or more recent multimodal image generators, which limits the scope of the claimed foundation for AR watermarking.

Important attack settings are acknowledged but not evaluated, especially geometric transforms such as crop, resize with shift, rotation, local edits, and adaptive attacks by an adversary who knows the clustering scheme and can re-encode or optimize token statistics to remove the watermark.

Image quality is mainly assessed by FID and a small set of visual examples. Since watermarking biases token selection and the paper notes it can change appearance, more direct perceptual or semantic fidelity measurements would better support the claim that image quality is preserved.

Reproducibility is partial from the manuscript alone: several perturbation implementations, exact package versions, and code details are deferred to a future repository, and code availability is promised rather than demonstrated in the submission.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: in-generation watermarking for discrete-token autoregressive image generators, which is less explored than watermarking for diffusion models.

The core idea of assigning visually similar codebook tokens to the same red/green cluster is simple, intuitive, and technically plausible as a way to reduce sensitivity to token reconstruction errors after image perturbations.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad within the chosen setting: LlamaGen GPT-B/GPT-L and RAR-XL, multiple perturbations, regeneration attacks, post-hoc watermark baselines, FID, ROC/AUC, TPR@1% FPR, runtime, and ablations over cluster count, watermark strength, green fraction, and hash prefix.

The results support the narrow claim that clustering improves robustness over naive token-level red-green watermarking, and that a perturbation-trained cluster classifier can further improve detection under several non-geometric perturbations.
weaknesses: A central technical concern is detector calibration. The method inherits a binomial p-value test, but the paper itself shows that green-token ratios for unwatermarked images can deviate substantially from the assumed null, especially with few clusters and some prefixes. Unequal cluster sizes and highly nonuniform AR token distributions make the probability of a green token generally not equal to gamma. This undermines the claimed statistical test and makes empirical ROC thresholds, rather than the proposed p-value, the real detector.

The prefix tuning procedure risks cherry-picking and weakens the evidence. The paper selects the best prefixes by evaluating robustness over perturbations, and the main tables use these selected prefixes. It is not clear that prefix selection is done on a separate validation set, nor how many trials are effectively searched. This can inflate robustness results and further conflicts with the claim of a clean statistical detector.

Originality is limited. The method is essentially red-green watermarking plus codebook clustering, with a cluster classifier variant similar in spirit to concurrent token reconstruction/robust verification methods. The contribution is useful but incremental, and the paper does not clearly separate what is novel from what is an expected adaptation of semantic/grouped-token watermarking.

The evaluation scope is narrower than the title and claims suggest. Experiments are limited to class-conditional ImageNet AR models with left-to-right discrete token generation. There is no evaluation on text-to-image AR models, masked/parallel token generation, modern multimodal AR systems, or out-of-domain image distributions.

Security evaluation is weak. The paper studies common corruptions and regeneration, but not adaptive attacks against the watermarking rule, prefix/key estimation, repeated querying, targeted token manipulation, detector-aware regeneration, or removal attacks exploiting the known clustering structure. For a watermarking paper, this is a material gap.

The method is not robust to geometric transformations such as crop, resize, rotation, or spatial misalignment; the authors acknowledge this only as future work. These transformations are common in real image sharing pipelines, so the practical robustness claim is incomplete.

The cluster classifier is trained with perturbations overlapping the evaluation perturbation family, so its strong gains partly reflect supervised robustness training for the tested corruptions. The paper does not convincingly establish generalization to unseen perturbations or stronger editing pipelines.

Image quality tradeoffs are not fully characterized. FID is reported, but the watermark visibly changes token composition and sometimes increases FID substantially at low cluster counts. The paper lacks stronger perceptual/user studies, CLIP/class fidelity metrics, or analysis of semantic degradation under watermark strength.

Comparison to baselines is imperfect. The main baselines are post-hoc watermarking methods with different capacity and threat models, while IndexMark is only evaluated for LlamaGen and not RAR. This makes the claimed superiority less decisive.

Presentation and reproducibility have several issues: algorithm notation has apparent mistakes, the text says the p-value should 'exceed' a threshold when rejection normally requires being below a threshold, there are typos and formatting problems, and important implementation details such as exact prefix-selection protocol and held-out splits are not sufficiently specified. Code is promised but not provided in the manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored problem: in-generation watermarking for discrete-token autoregressive image generators. Adapting red-green watermarking to AR image token sequences is natural, and the cluster-level variant is a simple, technically plausible response to token reconstruction instability under perturbations.

The empirical evaluation is substantial. The authors test LlamaGen GPT-B, LlamaGen GPT-L, and RAR-XL; include clean, common perturbation, and regeneration-attack settings; report AUC and TPR@FPR=1%; measure FID on 50k samples; and provide ablations over cluster count, watermark strength, green fraction, and hash prefix.

The results support the main practical claim that clustering similar visual tokens materially improves robustness over naive token-level red-green watermarking. The cluster classifier further improves difficult perturbations such as blur and salt-and-pepper noise, often outperforming the included post-hoc baselines.

The method is useful because verification is fast and does not require running the full AR generator. The runtime comparison shows verification costs comparable to lightweight post-hoc methods, which is an important practical advantage over some diffusion inversion-based watermarks.
The manuscript is generally clear, with a coherent motivation, algorithmic description, and meaningful supplementary details on perturbation settings, generation settings, sample counts, and compute.
weaknesses: The statistical detection story is weaker than the empirical ROC evaluation. The red-green p-value test assumes an unbiased binomial green-token count, but the paper itself shows that this assumption can fail, especially with few clusters and certain prefixes. Since clustered tokens and image-model token distributions introduce dependencies and non-uniformities, the theoretical calibration of p-values/FPR is not well justified; the work relies mostly on empirical calibration against generated negatives.

Prefix tuning raises protocol and robustness concerns. The paper selects the best-performing prefix after evaluating robustness over perturbations, but it is not fully separated from the reported evaluation distribution. This can overstate deployment performance under unseen perturbations, models, prompts/classes, or image distributions, and it also makes the security role of the prefix/key less clean.

The cluster classifier is trained with perturbation augmentations that overlap strongly with the evaluation perturbations. This is reasonable engineering, but it makes the gain partly perturbation-specific; the paper gives limited evidence for generalization to unseen transformations or realistic editing pipelines beyond the listed attacks.

The evaluation scope is still limited to class-conditional ImageNet AR generators with left-to-right discrete tokenization. It does not test modern text-to-image AR systems, different tokenizers/orderings, user editing workflows, or distribution shifts, so the breadth of the claimed relevance to AR image generation is not fully established.

Important attack settings are missing or acknowledged as failures: geometric transformations such as crop, resize, rotation, and zoom are not handled, and there is little adaptive attack analysis against an adversary aware of the clustering scheme or detector. For watermarking, these omissions are material even if they do not invalidate the contribution.

The comparisons are useful but not perfectly matched. Post-hoc baselines encode multi-bit messages and operate under different constraints, while the proposed method mainly tests detection/attribution through biased generation. IndexMark is only evaluated for LlamaGen because code/results are unavailable for RAR, limiting the strength of baseline conclusions.

Image utility is mostly assessed through FID and a few qualitative grids. Some low-cluster/high-penalty settings have severe FID degradation, and the paper provides limited analysis of semantic fidelity, class accuracy, prompt adherence, or human perceptual detectability of watermark-induced changes.

Reproducibility is good in spirit but incomplete at submission time: the authors promise code release and list settings/compute, but the exact repository and full implementation are not available in the manuscript. There are also minor presentation issues, including algorithm notation/typos and a likely sign error in describing p-value rejection, though these are not central to the contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored problem: in-generation watermarking for autoregressive image generators. Adapting KGW-style token watermarking to visual-token AR models is natural, and the core observation that token reconstruction instability hurts robustness is well motivated.

The proposed cluster-level watermark is simple and technically plausible: grouping codebook-neighboring visual tokens before red/green assignment directly targets the failure mode caused by perturbations moving decoded images to nearby codebook entries.

The evaluation is relatively broad for this area. Results cover LlamaGen GPT-B, LlamaGen GPT-L, and RAR-XL; multiple perturbations; regeneration attacks; post-hoc watermark baselines; and concurrent AR watermark baselines with available code.

The empirical gains are meaningful. The clustering variant improves substantially over the no-clustering token baseline, and the token/cluster classifier variants achieve strong TPR@1%FPR across many attacks while maintaining FID close to the unwatermarked generators in the main settings.

The paper includes useful ablations over cluster count, watermark strength, green-token fraction, prefix choice, runtime, CLIP/FID behavior, cluster initialization, and geometric transformations. The runtime results are also practically relevant, showing verification comparable to lightweight post-hoc methods.

The manuscript is mostly clear and reproducibility is aided by detailed generation settings, perturbation parameters, sample counts, training settings for the classifiers, and stated code availability.
weaknesses: The statistical/security foundation of prefix tuning is a concern. The method empirically selects hash prefixes because some prefixes induce high green counts on unwatermarked images. This suggests the nominal binomial test assumptions are not reliable for visual-token sequences. Although the authors use empirical ROC evaluation, the detection procedure and real deployment calibration depend on distribution-specific prefix selection, and the security discussion of reduced key space is fairly informal.

The threat model is limited. The paper assumes the AR backbone, VQ-VAE, and token/cluster predictor remain private and does not substantially evaluate adaptive removal or forgery attacks by an adversary with query access to generation/verification. For a watermarking paper, this leaves an important practical gap.

Robustness to geometric transformations is not intrinsic. Rotation, scaling, translation, perspective changes, and flipping can essentially destroy the watermark unless an external synchronization layer such as SyncSeal is used. This is acknowledged, but it weakens claims of broad robustness.

The evaluation is restricted to class-conditional ImageNet AR image models. The method is likely applicable beyond these cases, but the paper does not test text-to-image AR generators or more diverse prompt/content distributions, where token statistics and false-positive behavior may differ.

The trained token/cluster classifier variants require 100k generated images, perturbation-augmented training, and model-specific fine-tuning. These are reasonable costs, but the strongest results are not purely training-free and deployment complexity is higher than the main narrative sometimes suggests.

Image quality evidence is mostly FID/CLIP and visual examples. Because in-generation watermarking changes the sampled image rather than embedding into a fixed cover, it would be useful to measure class fidelity, semantic drift, or human preference more directly, especially for low cluster counts and high watermark strength.

Baseline comparability has some caveats: post-hoc methods encode random bitstrings and are evaluated through their own detectors, while the proposed method is a one-bit generative watermark with model access. The comparisons are useful but not perfectly apples-to-apples.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored problem: in-generation watermarking for autoregressive image generators, where direct transfer of LLM token watermarks is nontrivial because verification requires reconstructing visual tokens from pixels.

The core idea of assigning similar VQ tokens to the same red/green cluster is simple, technically plausible, and well motivated by the observed instability of token reconstruction under perturbations.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the proposed setting: three AR models, multiple perturbations, regeneration attacks, post-hoc watermark baselines, concurrent AR watermark baselines, FID/CLIP quality measurements, runtime, ablations over cluster count, watermark strength, green-token fraction, prefix choice, and cluster initialization.

The results support the main claim that clustering substantially improves robustness over the naive token-level KGW transfer, and that the token/cluster classifier further improves robustness, often with modest quality degradation at k=64.
The paper is generally clear, with a concrete algorithm and enough implementation detail to understand the method and reproduce the main design choices.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The method is largely KGW-style token watermarking plus k-means grouping in VQ codebook space, and related concurrent AR watermarking work also uses token reconstruction models. The paper’s main contribution is a useful adaptation rather than a conceptually deep new watermarking framework.

The evaluation is somewhat tuned to the proposed method. The hash prefix is selected empirically over candidate prefixes using validation perturbations, and the main results report this selected prefix rather than random-key or average-key performance. The paper acknowledges large prefix effects, especially at low cluster counts, but this remains a concern for robustness claims.

The security analysis is weak relative to watermarking claims. The threat model assumes private access to the AR backbone, VQ-VAE, and classifier, and there is little evaluation against adaptive removal or forgery attacks, verification-query attacks, collusion, or attackers aware of the clustering scheme. The statement that prefix tuning does not reduce practical security is mostly argued, not empirically or formally established.

Robustness to geometric transformations is poor without an external synchronization method; strong rotation, translation, perspective, flip, and scaling can nearly destroy detection. SyncSeal helps in supplementary experiments, but this makes the practical robustness partly dependent on an additional system not integrated into the core method.

The comparison to post-hoc baselines is not entirely apples-to-apples. Some baselines encode multi-bit payloads while the proposed method is effectively detecting a watermark signal; differences in payload, calibration, and operating assumptions could affect the fairness of the robustness comparison.

The method is evaluated only on class-conditional ImageNet AR generators with left-to-right discrete-token generation. It is unclear how well the approach transfers to modern text-to-image AR models, different tokenizers, non-raster generation orders, masked/parallel AR schemes, or higher-resolution open-world prompts.

The statistical test in the algorithm relies on a binomial green-count model, but the paper itself shows that unwatermarked green ratios can deviate substantially due to repeated visual structures and prefix choice. Empirical ROC calibration mitigates this in experiments, but the theoretical detection model is not fully reliable as stated.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored problem: in-generation watermarking for autoregressive image generators. Adapting KGW-style token watermarking to visual-token AR models is natural but nontrivial, and the proposed cluster-level red/green assignment is a simple, well-motivated fix for token reconstruction instability under image perturbations.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing for the claimed setting. Results cover LlamaGen GPT-B, LlamaGen GPT-L, and RAR-XL, include post-hoc and concurrent AR watermark baselines, and report both AUC and TPR@FPR=1% under JPEG, blur, Gaussian noise, salt-and-pepper noise, color jitter, and regeneration attacks.

The main result is strong: clustering substantially improves robustness over the naive token-level baseline while keeping image quality close to the unwatermarked generator in many settings, and the token/cluster classifier variants further improve difficult perturbations such as salt-and-pepper noise and color jitter.

The paper includes useful ablations over number of clusters, watermark strength, green-token fraction, prefix choice, and cluster initialization. These analyses make the method behavior more interpretable and expose real tradeoffs between robustness and image quality.

Runtime and reproducibility details are better than average: the paper reports verification latency, model/generation settings, perturbation settings, classifier training details, sample counts, compute, and baseline implementations.
weaknesses: The method has a notable dependence on empirical prefix tuning. The paper shows that some prefixes create heavy-tailed green-token ratios for unwatermarked images and increase false positives, especially with low cluster counts. This suggests the theoretical binomial p-value test is not well calibrated for visual-token sequences, whose spatial/token dependencies violate the independence and uniformity assumptions. The empirical ROC evaluation mitigates this in the paper but leaves deployment calibration less principled.

The best-performing variants rely on a trained token or cluster predictor using 100k generated images and perturbation-augmented fine-tuning. This is reasonable, but it weakens the simplicity/training-free story for the strongest results and may make robustness partly tied to the selected perturbation distribution.

Robustness to geometric transformations is weak without an external synchronization layer; the supplementary results indicate strong rotations, flips, perspective transforms, and scaling can essentially destroy the watermark. SyncSeal helps, but that adds another component and assumptions outside the core method.

The evaluation is limited to class-conditional, left-to-right AR image models and ImageNet-style generation. It remains unclear how well the approach transfers to text-to-image AR systems, different tokenizers, non-raster or parallel generation orders, or more diverse prompt distributions.

The threat model is mostly non-adaptive. The attacks are useful common perturbations and regenerations, but the paper does not evaluate an adversary aware of the clustering strategy, the detector, or the trained reconstruction model.

Image quality evidence is adequate but not exhaustive. FID is reported on 50k images and CLIP scores are summarized, but there is no human/perceptual study; some settings show non-negligible FID degradation, especially with fewer clusters or for RAR-XL clustering relative to the baseline generator.

The manuscript states that source code is available, but the extracted manuscript does not show an actual code URL. Given the large-scale evaluation and many implementation choices, reproducibility would benefit from a complete visible release link and exact scripts/configs.
